summary: Early Echo answers Flame in Freefall in two parts. A website that puts 1,939 records from 18 NASA microgravity fire experiments in one searchable table, ranks 35 groups of similar tests by how often the flame went out, maps every flame by oxygen and pressure, and uses small machine learning models, scored on test days they never saw, to predict which flames go out. It shows why early detection is really important: in NASA’s gas flame tests, 0 of 41 flames kept burning below 25% oxygen, but 18 of 21 small flames kept burning in 33 to 40% oxygen, a range that includes the 34% NASA recommends for Moon and Mars homes. The second part is a fire alarm made of sound. In orbit smoke doesn’t rise, but sound still crosses the room, and it travels faster through warm air. Our Android app turns two phones into a heat alarm by timing a sound sent between them both ways. A real candle made the sound arrive 2 to 4 microseconds early at a laptop’s microphone.
details:
The problem

Fire behaves differently in orbit. Nothing rises, so heat and smoke stay around a flame or drift wherever the fans push them, instead of rising to a detector on the ceiling. NASA's recommended air for Moon and Mars homes is 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi, so crews can go outside more often with less preparation. The space station keeps 21% oxygen at full pressure. More oxygen helps a fire. NASA has run nearly 2,000 fire tests in orbit, but the results sit in separate records, tables and papers, so it is hard to ask "would this flame keep burning in our air?"

Part 1:

We downloaded the records of all 24 fire experiments in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics archive and the 22 tables that list each test. After cleaning, 1,939 records from 18 experiments remain, and 613 of them say how the flame ended.

- Summarize: one searchable table of every test, each row linked to NASA's own record.

- Rank: 35 groups of similar tests (same experiment, fuel, pressure range and oxygen range), ranked by how often the flame went out on its own.

- Interpret: a map of every test by oxygen and pressure, with station air, the air used before a spacewalk and the planned habitat air marked. Click any point and it reads the nearest tests, or says "Too few to call".

- Predict: small machine-learning models, each scored on whole test days it never saw: gas flames 110 of 133 right (a simple nearest-tests rule got 116), droplets 186 of 206, inverse flames 118 of 139.

- Watch: a program read 130 of NASA's flame videos. In oxygen-rich air, flicker in a flame's last seconds told a dying flame from a steady one for 75 of 80 flames, looking back from the end of each test.

- 3D view: NASA's 3D model of the station's US Lab, with a fire the size of NASA's Saffire-I test placed in it. The spread of its heat there is our estimate.

What we found: below 25% oxygen, 0 of 41 gas flames kept burning. In 33 to 40% oxygen, 18 of 21 small flames did. So in NASA's tests, small gas flames kept burning in the air planned for the Moon and Mars, while they went out in station-like air. Finding a fire early matters more there.

Part 2:

Sound travels at about 343 m/s in room air, and about 0.6 m/s faster for each degree warmer. If the air along a 1 m line warms by 1 °C, a sound sent there and back returns about 10 microseconds sooner (a microsecond is a millionth of a second). A smoke detector waits for smoke to reach it, and a thermometer measures one spot. A sound line feels the whole path between two devices. Phones, laptops and speakers are already on board, so it needs no new hardware.

How the app works:

1. Install it on two Android phones on the same Wi-Fi or hotspot. They find each other by themselves.

2. Each phone plays a short, very high chirp (13 ms, 17 to 21 kHz) 23 times a second and records both phones' chirps. One chirp rises in pitch and the other falls, so they are never confused.

3. Each phone times the chirps far more finely than one audio sample (21 microseconds); in our simulation, to a fraction of a microsecond. The phones share their gaps over Wi-Fi and add them up. Clock offsets and wind cancel out; heat speeds the sound both ways, so it stays.

4. For the first 12 seconds the app learns the room's normal wobble. The alarm level is 6 times that, and never less than 1 microsecond.

5. If the sound arrives early by more than that for 1 second, both screens turn orange. A hand or a person in the line makes the sound late instead, and the app says "Something's in the way".

A debug screen shows every reading, and each test can be saved. A "Not a flame" button marks people, hands and fans, so a later model can learn to tell them apart from fire.

How we tested it

- A real candle: one laptop played a chirp through a soundbar about 0.9 m away and recorded it with its own two microphones, with a candle under the middle of the line. Each of the 3 times we lit it, the sound arrived early: 2 to 4 microseconds at one microphone and 1 to 2 at the other. One cut sorted 115 of 117 seconds right as lit or out at the first microphone, but we set that cut on the same recording, so it is not a blind test. This was one laptop timing one way, and on Earth the heat rises into the line.

- Nine simulated tests: two simulated phones 1 m apart with drifting clocks, echoes, noise and Wi-Fi delay. A small heat change sets off both phones; a gust of wind, slow warming, a hand and a standing person do not. All nine pass.

- A 3D estimate: in NASA's US Lab model, with six sound lines between four laptops and the station's air flow, a Saffire-I-sized fire trips the first line after about 10 seconds and 4 of 6 lines within 2 minutes. This comes from a model, not a measurement.

Limits

The phone app has not been tested on a real flame, and nothing has been tested in orbit. A fire's heat has to cross a sound line to be seen. A smouldering fire with little heat may not show, and a warm person near the line can shift it almost as much as a candle, so an alarm means "go and look". NASA has few tests near habitat air, and the site marks where a model is guessing.

Our future plans

1. A blind flame test with the phones in a safe lab: one person lights the flame or doesn't, another reads the screen.

2. More than two phones, so sound lines cross the whole room.

3. A model that tells a flame from a person or a fan, trained on saved tests.

4. The same app on the laptops and speakers already aboard the station, as an early second opinion next to the smoke detectors.

Tools

Python with numpy and scikit-learn (data and models), ffmpeg (video reading), React, TypeScript, Vite and three.js (website), Kotlin and the Android SDK (phone app). No special hardware: two Android phones, or a laptop and a speaker.
